title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works (Google Search Central)
text:
## The three stages of Google Search

Google Search works in three stages, and not all pages make it through each stage. Crawling: Google downloads text, images, and videos from pages it found on the internet with automated programs called crawlers. Indexing: Google analyzes the text, images, and video files on the page, and stores the information in the Google index, which is a large database. Serving search results: when a user searches, Google returns information relevant to the query.

## Crawling

The first stage is finding out what pages exist on the web. There is no central registry of all web pages, so Google must constantly look for new and updated pages and add them to its list of known pages. This process is called URL discovery. Some pages are known because Google has already visited them. Other pages are discovered when Google follows a link from a known page to a new page, or when a site owner submits a sitemap. Once Google discovers a page URL, it may visit (crawl) the page to find out what is on it. Googlebot uses an algorithmic process to determine which sites to crawl, how often, and how many pages to fetch from each site. Googlebot does not crawl all the pages it discovered: some pages may be disallowed for crawling by the site owner, and others may not be accessible without logging in. During the crawl, Google renders the page and runs any JavaScript it finds using a recent version of Chrome, which is important because sites rely on JavaScript to bring content to the page. Crawling depends on whether Googlebot can access the site: common problems include server issues, network issues, and robots.txt rules preventing access.

## Indexing

After a page is crawled, Google tries to understand what the page is about. This stage is called indexing and it includes processing and analyzing the textual content and key content tags and attributes, such as title elements and alt attributes, images, videos, and more. During indexing, Google determines if a page is a duplicate of another page on the internet or canonical. The canonical is the page that may be shown in search results. To select the canonical, Google groups together (clusters) the pages found on the internet that have similar content, and selects the one that is most representative of the group. Google then collects signals about the canonical page and its contents, which may be used in the next stage. Some pages are not indexed: the content quality may be low, robots meta rules may disallow indexing, or the design of the website may make indexing difficult.

## Serving search results

When a user enters a query, Google searches the index for matching pages and returns the results believed to be the highest quality and most relevant. Relevancy is determined by hundreds of factors, which could include information such as the user's location, language, and device (desktop or phone). Ranking is done by algorithms, and Google does not accept payment to rank pages higher. For a given query, the search features shown change based on what is most relevant.

title: Introduction to robots.txt (Google Search Central)
text:
## What a robots.txt file is for

A robots.txt file tells search engine crawlers which URLs the crawler can access on your site. This is used mainly to avoid overloading your site with requests; it is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google. To keep a web page out of Google, block indexing with noindex or password-protect the page.

## What robots.txt does and does not do

For web pages, robots.txt manages crawling traffic if you think your server will be overwhelmed by requests from Googlebot, or to avoid crawling unimportant or similar pages on your site. Important warning: a robots.txt file is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google search results. If other pages point to your page with descriptive text, Google could still index the URL without visiting the page. If you want to block your page from search results, use another method such as password protection or a noindex tag.

For media files, you can use robots.txt to manage crawl traffic and to prevent image, video, and audio files from appearing in Google search results. This does not prevent other pages or users from linking to your image, video, or audio file. For resource files such as unimportant image, script, or style files, you can use robots.txt to block them if you think that pages loaded without these resources will not be significantly affected by the loss. However, if the absence of these resources makes the page harder for Googlebot to understand, do not block them.

## Limitations

The instructions in robots.txt files cannot enforce crawler behavior to your site; it is up to the crawler to obey them. While Googlebot and other respectable web crawlers obey the instructions, other crawlers might not. Different crawlers interpret syntax differently. A page that is disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites. To reliably block a URL from appearing in results, use the noindex rule, which requires that the page not be blocked by robots.txt so the crawler can see the rule.

title: Learn about sitemaps (Google Search Central)
text:
## What a sitemap is

A sitemap is a file where you provide information about the pages, videos, and other files on your site, and the relationships between them. Search engines like Google read this file to crawl your site more efficiently. A sitemap tells Google which pages and files you think are important, and also provides valuable information about these files. For example, when the page was last updated and any alternate language versions of the page.

## When you might need a sitemap

You might need a sitemap if your site is really large, because Google web crawlers might overlook crawling some of your new or recently updated pages. Your site has a large archive of content pages that are isolated or not well linked to each other; if your site pages do not naturally reference each other, you can list them in a sitemap to ensure Google does not overlook some of your pages. Your site is new and has few external links to it; Googlebot and other web crawlers crawl the web by following links from one page to another, so Google might not discover your pages if no other sites link to them. Your site has a lot of rich media content (video, images) or is shown in Google News; Google can take additional information from sitemaps into account for Search.

## When you might not need a sitemap

You might not need a sitemap if your site is small, meaning about 500 pages or fewer on your site (only pages you think need to be in search results count toward this total). Your site is comprehensively linked internally, meaning Google can find all the important pages on your site by following links starting from the home page. You do not have many media files (video, image) or news pages that you want to show in search results. Sitemaps do not guarantee that all the items included will be crawled and indexed, as Google processes rely on complex algorithms, but in most cases your site will benefit from having a sitemap.

title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel=canonical and other methods (Google Search Central)
text:
## What a canonical URL is

A canonical URL is the URL of the page that Google chose as the most representative from a set of duplicate pages. Often called deduplication, this process helps Google show only one version of the otherwise duplicate content in its search results. There are many reasons why a site can have duplicate content, including region variants, device variants, protocol variants (HTTP vs HTTPS), site functions such as sorting and filtering, and syndicated content.

## Why choose a canonical URL

You want to tell Google which URL to show in search results, consolidate link signals for similar or duplicate pages so signals from multiple URLs help the single preferred URL, simplify tracking metrics for a single product or topic, and manage syndicated content. Even if you do not explicitly tell Google your preferred canonical URL, Google will identify what it considers the best version, but you can influence the choice.

## Methods to specify a canonical, in order of strength

Use redirects: a permanent redirect (301 or 308) sends a strong signal that the redirect target should become canonical. Use rel="canonical" link annotations, either as an HTML link element in the head or as an HTTP header. List the canonical in a sitemap, which is a weaker signal but easy for large sites. You can combine methods, but do not send contradictory signals.

## Best practices and pitfalls

Use absolute URLs, not relative paths, in canonical annotations. Add a self-referencing canonical to the canonical page. Do not use the robots.txt file or the URL removal tool for canonicalization purposes. Do not specify different URLs as canonical for the same page using different methods. Within your site, link to the canonical URL rather than a duplicate URL. Google prefers HTTPS pages over HTTP pages and prefers URLs included in an hreflang cluster.

title: Spam policies for Google web search (Google Search Central)
text:
## Google web search spam policies

These policies cover the behaviors and tactics that can lead to a page or an entire site being ranked lower or completely omitted from Google Search.

Cloaking: presenting different content to users and search engines with the intent to manipulate search rankings and mislead users. For example, showing a page about travel destinations to search engines while showing a page about discount drugs to users.

Doorway abuse: sites or pages created to rank for specific, similar search queries that lead users to intermediate pages that are not as useful as the final destination.

Expired domain abuse: buying an expired domain and repurposing it primarily to manipulate rankings by hosting content that provides little to no value to users. For example, affiliate content on a site previously used by a government agency.

Hacked content: any content placed on a site without permission, due to vulnerabilities in a site's security, including injected content, added pages, and redirects.

Hidden text and links: placing content on a page in a way solely to manipulate search engines and not easily viewable by human visitors, such as white text on a white background, or hiding text behind an image, or using CSS to position text off-screen.

Keyword stuffing: filling a page with keywords or numbers in an attempt to manipulate rankings, often appearing as an unnatural list of words. For example, repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural.

Link spam: links created primarily for the purpose of manipulating rankings, including buying or selling links for ranking purposes, excessive link exchanges, and using automated programs or services to create links.

Machine-generated traffic: consuming Google Search resources, or sending automated queries, including scraping results for rank-checking or other automated access to Search conducted without express permission.

Scaled content abuse: generating many pages primarily for manipulating search rankings and not helping users, whether created through automation, human effort, or a combination, including using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value.

Scraped content: taking content from other sites, often automatically, and republishing it without adding original content or value, or modifying it only slightly.

Site reputation abuse: publishing third-party pages with little or no first-party oversight primarily to manipulate rankings by taking advantage of the host site's ranking signals. For example, a third party publishing payday-loan reviews on a trusted educational site.

Sneaky redirects: maliciously redirecting a user to a different page than the one they initially requested, such as showing desktop users a normal page while redirecting mobile users to a spam domain.

Thin affiliation: pages with product affiliate links where product descriptions and reviews are copied directly from the original merchant without original content or added value.

User-generated spam: spammy content added to a site by users, such as spammy accounts on hosting services, spammy posts on forum threads, comment spam, and spammy files uploaded to file hosting platforms.

title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google Search results (Google Search Central)
text:
## Core Web Vitals and page experience

Core Web Vitals are a set of metrics that measure real-world user experience for loading performance, interactivity, and visual stability of the page. Google recommends site owners achieve good Core Web Vitals for success with Search and to ensure a great user experience generally.

## The three metrics and their good thresholds

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance. To provide a good user experience, LCP should occur within the first 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness. To provide a good user experience, pages should have an INP of less than 200 milliseconds.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability. To provide a good user experience, pages should maintain a CLS score of less than 0.1.

## Relationship to ranking

Google's guidance states that great page experience, which Core Web Vitals contribute to, aligns with what Google's core ranking systems seek to reward. There is no single page experience ranking signal, and good page experience is not a magic bullet: content still needs to be helpful and relevant. Achieving good Core Web Vitals supports success in Search and a great user experience. The metrics are measured on real users (field data) rather than only in lab tests.

title: Influencing your title links in search results (Google Search Central)
text:
## What a title link is

A title link is the title of a search result on Google Search and other properties (for example, Google News) that links to the web page. Google uses a number of different sources to automatically determine the title link, including the content in the title element, main visual title shown on the page, heading elements such as h1, other content that is large and prominent through the use of style treatments, anchor text on the page, text within links that point to the page, and WebSite structured data.

## Best practices for a good title element

Make sure every page on your site has a title specified in the title element. Write descriptive and concise text: avoid vague descriptions like "Home" for your home page or "Profile" for a specific person's profile, and avoid unnecessarily long or verbose text. Avoid keyword stuffing: it is sometimes helpful to have a few descriptive terms in the title element, but there is no reason to repeat the same words or phrases multiple times. Avoid repeated or boilerplate text: use unique titles that describe each page, rather than the same text across many pages. Brand your titles concisely: the title element for the home page is a reasonable place to include some additional information about your site, but displaying that text in the title of every single page hurts readability.

## Common problems Google fixes with a different title

Google may show a different title link than the title element if the title element is half-empty (for example "| Site Name"), obsolete (contains an old date the page no longer refers to), inaccurate (does not describe the page well), micro-boilerplate (repeated across a set of similar pages), or in a different language or script than the main content. There is no limit on how long a title element can be, but the title link may be truncated to fit the device width. Blocking a page with robots.txt does not prevent it from being indexed if other pages link to it, so use noindex to keep a page out of results.

title: Intro to how structured data markup works (Google Search Central)
text:
## What structured data is

Structured data is a standardized format for providing information about a page and classifying the page content. For example, on a recipe page, structured data describes what the ingredients are, the cooking time and temperature, the calories, and so on. Google uses structured data to understand the content on the page and to enable special search result features and enhancements called rich results.

## Rich results and the business case

Many Google Search features are eligible only when structured data is present. Google cites case studies: Nestle found that pages that show as rich results in Search have an 82% higher click-through rate than non-rich result pages, and Rotten Tomatoes measured a 25% higher click-through rate for pages with structured data.

## Supported formats

Google Search supports structured data in three formats: JSON-LD, which is a JavaScript notation embedded in a script tag in the page head or body and is recommended because it is the easiest to implement and maintain at scale; Microdata, an open-community HTML specification that uses HTML tag attributes; and RDFa, an HTML5 extension that uses tag attributes. Most Google structured data uses schema.org vocabulary, but Google Search behavior is defined by the Google Search Central documentation rather than schema.org.

## Quality guidelines

Include all required properties; an object missing a required property is not eligible for rich results. It is more important to supply fewer but complete and accurate recommended properties than to try to provide every possible recommended property with less complete, badly formed, or inaccurate data. Structured data must be a faithful representation of the page content visible to users, must not be hidden, and must not mark up content that is irrelevant or misleading. Violating the structured data guidelines can make a page ineligible for rich results or trigger a manual action.

title: Google Search Essentials (Google Search Central)
text:
## Google Search Essentials

Google Search Essentials describes the core parts of what makes your web-based content (web pages, images, videos, or other publicly available material that Google finds on the web) eligible to appear and perform well on Google Search. It is made up of three parts.

Technical requirements: what Google needs from a web page to show it in Google Search. There are actually very few technical things you need to do to a web page; most sites pass the technical requirements without even realizing it. In summary, Googlebot must be able to access the page (it is not blocked and does not require login for public content), the page must return a successful HTTP status code, and the page must have indexable content that is not blocked by noindex.

Spam policies: the behaviors and tactics that can lead to a page or an entire site being ranked lower or completely omitted from Google Search. Sites that focus on providing a good user experience and quality content, in line with Google's guidance, tend to perform well.

Key best practices: the main things that can help improve how your site appears in Google Search results. These include creating helpful, reliable, people-first content; using words that people would use to look for your content and placing them in prominent locations like the title, main heading, and alt text; making links crawlable so Google can find pages by following links; telling people about your site to build awareness; and following best practices for images, video, structured data, and JavaScript. Following the Search Essentials does not guarantee ranking, but violating the spam policies or failing the technical requirements can prevent a page from appearing at all.

title: Block search indexing with noindex (Google Search Central)
text:
## The noindex rule

You can prevent a page or other resource from appearing in Google Search by including a noindex rule in the page. When Googlebot next crawls that page and sees the tag or header, Google drops that page entirely from Google Search results, regardless of whether other sites link to it.

## Two ways to implement noindex

You can implement noindex as a meta tag or as an HTTP response header, and both have the same effect. To prevent most search engine crawlers from indexing a page, place a meta tag in the head section of the page: meta name=robots content=noindex. To address only Google's crawlers, use meta name=googlebot content=noindex. Note that some search engines may interpret the noindex rule differently, so it is possible that a page might still appear in results from other search engines.

Alternatively, use the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header with a value of noindex. A response header can be used for non-HTML resources such as PDFs, video files, and image files where a meta tag cannot be placed in HTML.

## Critical warning: do not block the page with robots.txt

For the noindex rule to be effective, the page or resource must not be blocked by a robots.txt file, and it has to be otherwise accessible to the crawler. If the page is blocked by a robots.txt file, or the crawler cannot access the page, the crawler will never see the noindex rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it. Use the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to verify that Google can fetch the page and see the noindex rule.

title: Control your snippets in search results and meta descriptions (Google Search Central)
text:
## What a snippet is

A snippet is the description or summary part of a search result on Google Search and other properties. Google uses a number of different sources to automatically create snippets, primarily deriving them from the content of the page itself. Google sometimes uses the meta description HTML element from a page to generate a snippet if it might give users a more accurate description of the page than content taken directly from the page.

## The meta description tag

The meta description tag (meta name=description) generally informs and interests users with a short, relevant summary of what a particular page is about. It is like a pitch that convinces the user that the page is exactly what they are looking for. There is no limit on how long a meta description can be, but the snippet is truncated as needed to fit the device width.

## Best practices for meta descriptions

Create unique descriptions for each page; identical or similar descriptions across every page are not helpful when individual pages appear in results. Include clearly tagged, relevant information such as, for a news or blog post, the author, date of publication, or byline, and for a product page, key facts like price, age, and manufacturer. Programmatically generate descriptions for database-driven or hard-to-write-individually sites, keeping them varied and human readable, and avoid descriptions that are just a long string of keywords or duplicate the entire page content.

## Controlling snippet display

Use the nosnippet rule to prevent a text snippet from being shown at all. Use max-snippet:[number] to specify a maximum text length in characters. Use the data-nosnippet HTML attribute on a span, div, or section to exclude specific parts of a page from the snippet. These robots meta rules control snippet length and content but do not affect ranking.

title: What Is Search Intent and the Three Cs (Ahrefs)
text:
## What search intent is

Search intent (also called user intent or keyword intent) is the reason behind a searcher's query: what they are trying to accomplish. Ranking well in Google today requires matching the dominant intent of a keyword, because Google's job is to serve the results that best satisfy searchers.

## The four types of search intent

Informational: the searcher is looking for information or an answer to a specific question, for example "how to tie a tie" or "what is search intent." Navigational: the searcher is looking for a specific website or page, for example "ahrefs login" or "facebook." Commercial: the searcher is comparing products or services and doing research before making a purchase decision, for example "best air fryer" or "ahrefs vs semrush." Transactional: the searcher is ready to complete an action, often a purchase, for example "buy iphone 15" or "nike air max coupon."

## The three Cs of search intent

To optimize a page for intent, study the top-ranking results and match three things. Content type: the dominant type of content ranking, such as blog post, product page, category page, or landing page. Content format: the structural style of the top results, such as how-to guide, step-by-step tutorial, list post, opinion piece, review, or comparison. Content angle: the dominant selling point or hook of the ranking pages, which reveals what searchers value, for example current-year freshness in "best" queries. For the query "best air fryer," the type is blog posts, the format is list posts, and the angle is up-to-date current-year recommendations.

## Optimizing for intent

Analyze what already ranks rather than guessing, because Google's rankings are a real-time reflection of intent. If the results are a mix of content types, intent may be ambiguous or mixed. Do not try to force a transactional page to rank for an informational query, and vice versa.

title: Internal Links for SEO Best Practices (Ahrefs)
text:
## What internal links are and why they matter

An internal link is a link that points from one page on a domain to a different page on the same domain. Internal links help visitors navigate a website, establish an information hierarchy, and spread ranking power (link equity, historically PageRank) around the site. Google's John Mueller has said internal linking is super critical for SEO and one of the biggest things you can do to help Google understand what pages you consider important.

## The three roles of internal links

Discovery and crawlability: search engines find new pages by following links, so a page with no internal links pointing to it (an orphan page) is hard for Google to discover unless it is in the sitemap or has external backlinks. Authority flow: internal links pass PageRank; the more internal links a page receives (especially from high-authority pages), the stronger the signal that it is important. Context: descriptive anchor text tells Google what the linked page is about, so anchors like "red maxi dresses" are far more useful than "click here."

## Best practices

Add contextual internal links within the body content where they genuinely help the reader. Use descriptive, relevant anchor text rather than generic phrases. Link from pages with authority (they carry more weight) to the pages you most want to rank. Keep important pages within a few clicks of the home page in a logical hierarchy. Fix orphan pages by adding internal links to them. Do not overdo it: too many links on one page dilutes the value each passes, and do not add noindex or nofollow to pages you actually want indexed and ranked.

## Common mistakes

Orphan pages with no internal links, generic anchor text such as "click here," linking only from low-authority pages, over-linking a single page, and relying on navigation or footer links alone instead of contextual in-content links.

title: Backlinks: The Definitive Guide (Backlinko)
text:
## What a backlink is

A backlink is any link from another website that points to yours. Also called inbound links or incoming links, backlinks help build authority and brand awareness across search engines and, increasingly, AI platforms. Backlinks remain a core Google ranking signal: a Backlinko analysis of 11.8 million Google search results found that the number one result has 3.8 times more backlinks than the pages ranked number 2 through 10.

## What makes a high-quality backlink

Topical relevance: links carry more value when the linking page, its surrounding content, and the anchor text all align with your industry or topic. Context matters more than domain authority alone. Source credibility (authority): evaluate whether the linking site has real organic traffic, genuine editorial standards such as named authors and bylines, and a healthy backlink profile of its own from other credible sources. Editorial placement: earned links, where an editor genuinely chooses to cite you, outweigh paid or exchanged links; properly disclosed paid or sponsored links should use the rel="sponsored" attribute, and links you do not vouch for should use rel="nofollow" or rel="ugc." Link status and diversity: dofollow links traditionally pass ranking equity, and a natural profile includes a mix of link types and anchors rather than an unnatural pattern.

## Link building tactics

Become a helpful expert source that journalists cite. Create genuinely link-worthy assets such as original data studies, free tools, and calculators that other sites naturally reference. Run broken link building by finding dead links on relevant pages and offering your working resource as the replacement. Avoid buying links or participating in link schemes, which violate Google's spam policies and can trigger a manual action or algorithmic devaluation.

title: SERP Features: What They Are and How to Get Them (Ahrefs)
text:
## What SERP features are

SERP features are the elements of a search engine results page that are not traditional organic search results. They can push the traditional blue links down the page and change how much organic traffic a top ranking earns. According to Ahrefs data, 99% of search queries trigger at least one SERP feature; sitelinks appear in around 95% of queries and image packs in around 39%.

## Common SERP features

Featured snippets: an answer box pulled from a ranking page, in paragraph, list, table, or video format, that answers the query directly at the top. Knowledge panel: an informational card about an entity such as a person, company, or place. People Also Ask: an expandable box of related questions. Sitelinks: extra links to other pages on the same site shown under the main result. Image pack: a horizontal row of images. Local pack: the top three local business results shown with a map. Top stories: a carousel of recent news. Video results and video features. Shopping and product results: product listings with prices. Ads at the top and bottom of the page.

## How to optimize for SERP features

For featured snippets, target keywords that already trigger a snippet, format the answer concisely, and answer the question immediately and clearly. For sitelinks, use strong internal linking, clear page titles, and a logical site structure. For image packs, use descriptive filenames, alt text, captions, and an image sitemap. For the local pack, optimize your Google Business Profile, keep name-address-phone citations consistent, and earn reviews. Because features can reduce clicks to organic results (zero-click searches), factor them into whether a keyword is worth targeting.

title: Long Tail Keywords: How to Find and Use Them (Backlinko)
text:
## What long-tail keywords are

Long-tail keywords are search terms with relatively low search volume and competition levels. They tend to be longer in length, three to five or more words, than most other keyword types. The name comes from the search demand curve: any individual long-tail query gets few searches, but collectively they make up a large chunk of all Google searches. Backlinko notes that 92% of all keywords get 10 or fewer searches per month, which is the long tail of the distribution.

## Why they are valuable

Lower competition: long-tail keywords are much less competitive than shorter head keywords, so they are easier to rank for despite lower individual search volume. More specific intent: the extra words reveal exactly what the searcher wants, so the intent is clearer. Higher conversion: because long-tail searchers are often further along in the buying cycle and know precisely what they want, traffic from long-tail terms tends to convert really well.

## How to find and use them

Finding methods include Google's "Searches related to" section, Google Autocomplete suggestions, People Also Ask boxes, Answer the Public for question keywords, forums and discussion boards, Google Search Console performance reports for queries you already get impressions on, and Google Trends. To use them, you can either create dedicated content optimized around a single valuable long-tail term, or naturally incorporate several related long-tail variations into a broader piece targeting a medium or head keyword, since a single strong page can rank for hundreds of long-tail variations.

title: Email sender guidelines (Google / Gmail Help)
text:
## Email sender guidelines

To help ensure Gmail users continue to receive email that is safe, reliable, and secure, Google introduced requirements for senders sending email to Gmail accounts, with core requirements enforced from February 1, 2024.

## Requirements for all senders

Every sender that sends email to Gmail accounts must: set up SPF or DKIM email authentication for their domains; ensure that sending domains or IPs have valid forward and reverse DNS records, also referred to as PTR records; use a TLS connection for transmitting email; keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.30% and avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher; format messages according to the Internet Message Format standard (RFC 5322); do not impersonate Gmail From: headers, which will start getting a From: header rewrite; and if you regularly forward email, add ARC headers and a List-id header to messages.

## Additional requirements for senders of 5,000 or more messages per day

A bulk sender is any sender that sends close to 5,000 messages or more to Gmail accounts within a 24 hour period. Bulk senders must additionally: set up SPF and DKIM email authentication for their domains (both, not just one); set up DMARC email authentication for their sending domain, and the DMARC policy can be set to none; for direct mail, the domain in the sender's From: header must be aligned with either the SPF domain or the DKIM domain, which is required to pass DMARC alignment; and marketing messages and subscribed messages must support one-click unsubscribe and include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the message body.

## Spam rate guidance

Google recommends senders keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher. A high spam rate can cause messages to be marked as spam or rejected. Maintaining a low spam rate helps senders be more resilient to occasional spikes in user complaints. These requirements apply to messages sent to personal Gmail accounts, not necessarily Google Workspace accounts.

title: Email sender guidelines: one-click unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe headers (Google Workspace Admin Help)
text:
## One-click unsubscribe for bulk senders

For senders sending more than 5,000 messages per day, marketing messages and subscribed messages must support one-click unsubscribe and include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the message body.

## The headers required

To set up one-click unsubscribe, include both of these headers in outgoing messages: a List-Unsubscribe-Post header with the value List-Unsubscribe=One-Click, and a List-Unsubscribe header containing the URL that processes the unsubscribe request, for example List-Unsubscribe: <https://example.com/unsubscribe/example>. When the recipient clicks unsubscribe, Gmail sends a POST request to the URL specified in the List-Unsubscribe header, with the body List-Unsubscribe=One-Click. These headers conform to RFC 8058 and RFC 2369.

## Processing unsubscribe requests

Senders must let recipients opt out of receiving mail, and process unsubscription requests within 2 days. The one-click unsubscribe requirement applies to promotional and subscribed marketing messages, not to transactional messages such as receipts. You should still include a visible unsubscribe link in the body of the message in addition to the header, so recipients can easily opt out.

## Spam rate thresholds

Google recommends senders keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10%, and to avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher. Reaching or exceeding 0.30% can cause a temporary or permanent increase in the filtering or rejection of a sender's messages. A consistently low spam rate, combined with proper authentication and easy unsubscription, is the foundation of good inbox placement under the 2024 bulk sender rules.

title: Sender Best Practices and bulk sender requirements (Yahoo Postmaster / Yahoo Senders)
text:
## Yahoo sender requirements

Yahoo, in coordination with the broader industry, introduced sender requirements that took effect in early 2024. They parallel Gmail's requirements so senders can meet a single bar.

## Requirements for all senders

All senders must implement SPF or DKIM at a minimum, maintain valid forward and reverse DNS (PTR) records for sending IPs, and comply with RFC 5321 and RFC 5322. Keep your spam rate below 0.3%, measured against mail delivered to the inbox.

## Additional requirements for bulk senders

Bulk senders must implement both SPF and DKIM, and publish a valid DMARC policy with at least p=none, and DMARC must pass. The domain in the From: header must be in alignment with the SPF or DKIM domain. Including a rua tag in the DMARC record to receive aggregate reports is strongly recommended. Bulk senders must implement a functioning List-Unsubscribe header that supports one-click unsubscribe; the POST method described in RFC 8058 is highly recommended. Include a visible unsubscribe link in the email body and honor unsubscribes within 2 days.

## General best practices

Send mail only to users who explicitly requested it, and use confirmed opt-in (double opt-in) to verify subscriptions. Respect your intended sending frequency and avoid unexpected volume increases. Do not purchase mailing lists. Monitor bounces and remove inactive recipients. Enroll in the Complaint Feedback Loop (CFL) for your DKIM-signed mail. Send periodic reconfirmation emails to inactive subscribers. Segregate bulk and marketing mail from transactional mail by using different IPs or DKIM domains, publish meaningful reverse DNS, and keep mail servers patched and secured.

title: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC explained (Litmus)
text:
## The three email authentication protocols

Email authentication proves to receiving servers that a message genuinely comes from the domain it claims to, and is the first step in building trust with mailbox providers. Three protocols work together.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): domain owners publish a DNS record that specifies which mail servers are authorized to send messages using their domain. Receiving mail servers verify that an incoming message originated from a sending IP address listed in the domain's SPF record.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): a cryptographic signature is attached to outgoing messages. This signature lets the receiver verify that the domain owner authorized the message and that the message content was not altered in transit. DKIM lets an organization claim responsibility for a message in a way that can be validated.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance): DMARC is essentially a policy and reporting layer on top of DKIM and SPF. It lets a domain owner tell receivers what to do with mail that fails authentication, and it provides reports.

## How DMARC ties them together

Inbox providers that support DMARC attempt to validate both DKIM and SPF. DMARC adds two critical capabilities beyond SPF and DKIM alone. First, alignment: under DMARC the domain used in DKIM or SPF must match (be in alignment with) the domain in the visible From: header, which is what actually prevents spoofing, because an attacker can pass raw SPF or DKIM on their own domain but cannot align it with your From: address. Second, policy enforcement: the domain owner sets a policy of none (monitor only), quarantine (send failing mail to spam), or reject (block failing mail outright). DMARC also delivers aggregate reports (via the rua tag) showing message volume, sources, and authentication results, so senders can see who is sending mail as their domain before tightening the policy.

title: The Marketer's Guide to Email Deliverability (Litmus)
text:
## Deliverability vs delivery vs inbox placement

Email deliverability is whether your message actually reaches a subscriber's inbox rather than the spam or promotions folder. It is distinct from delivery, which only confirms that the recipient's mail server accepted the message without bouncing. Inbox placement rate (IPR) is the percentage of delivered emails that actually land in the inbox versus the spam folder, and it is the true measure of deliverability success. A high delivery rate can still hide a poor inbox placement rate.

## What influences deliverability

Authentication: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verify your legitimacy, and BIMI (optional) can add your logo. Sender reputation: mailbox providers track the reputation of your sending IP and your domain, built from subscriber engagement (opens, clicks, replies), sending behavior (consistent volume and frequency), and list hygiene. New IPs require gradual volume ramp-up, called IP warming. Engagement signals: opens and clicks tell providers your mail is wanted, while a lack of engagement suggests unwanted mail. List quality: invalid addresses, spam traps, and blocklists damage reputation. Spam complaints: high complaint rates signal poor practices, so make unsubscribing easy to prevent complaints.

## Best practices to reach the inbox

Build a subscriber-first strategy, personalize and segment content, maintain list hygiene through regular cleaning, use double opt-in to verify addresses, run re-engagement campaigns for subscribers who have gone quiet (for example around 60 days), honor unsubscribe requests immediately, implement proper authentication, monitor sender reputation continuously, use pre-send testing to catch spam and rendering risks, and monitor placement after sending. A healthy program targets full inbox placement, with a 90%+ inbox placement rate considered a healthy baseline.

title: Email List Hygiene: How to Build a Clean Email List (Litmus)
text:
## What list hygiene is and why it matters

Email list hygiene is the practice of maintaining a database of valid, engaged subscribers by removing invalid addresses and inactive contacts. Data quality is one of the variables mailbox providers look at when deciding what to do with your mail: if a list is clean of invalid data, and other variables like IP reputation, content, and engagement are strong, a message is likely to reach the inbox. Sending to a compromised list results in severely underperforming campaigns, a spike in complaint rates, and possible blocklisting, because dead and purchased addresses often contain spam traps.

## What to remove

Unsubscribes: remove immediately as an ethical practice, even though CAN-SPAM technically allows up to 10 business days. Hard bounces: invalid addresses that do not exist should be removed right away. Role addresses: generic accounts such as info@ and sales@ indicate lower list quality. Old or dead domains: outdated email services suggest stale data. Soft bounces: monitor temporary failures and remove an address after roughly 3 consecutive failed campaigns or a month of persistent problems.

## Invalid address types and risky sources

Invalid addresses fall into bad format (malformed address), bad domain (no mail server for the domain), and bad account (nonexistent username at a valid domain). High-risk collection methods such as point-of-sale and mobile signups produce elevated invalid rates due to manual entry errors and autocorrect.

## Sunset policies and re-engagement

Establish a sunset policy that suppresses or removes chronically unengaged subscribers; a common rule of thumb is to target subscribers who have not opened or clicked in 3 to 12 months. Before removing them, run an automated re-engagement or re-permission campaign to win back or confirm interest. Build lists through website conversions, offline events, and proper verification, and never purchase pre-built lists.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Dark Mode for Email Marketers (Litmus)
text:
## What dark mode does

Dark mode uses light-colored typography, UI elements, and icons on dark backgrounds. Users like it because it reduces eye strain, saves battery life on OLED screens, and can improve legibility in low light. For email marketers the challenge is that email clients apply dark mode inconsistently, so an email designed only for light mode can break.

## Three ways clients handle dark mode

No color change: some clients (for example Apple Mail and Gmail on desktop, AOL, Yahoo Mail) apply dark mode to their own interface but render the email itself unchanged unless the designer opts in.

Partial color inversion: clients such as Outlook.com and the Outlook app on iOS and Android detect areas with light backgrounds and invert them, while leaving already-dark backgrounds alone.

Full color inversion: clients such as Gmail app on iOS, Outlook 2021 and Office 365 on Windows, and Windows Mail invert all colors, so even elements that were already dark become light, which can break carefully designed emails.

## Best practices

Use transparent PNGs for logos and icons, and add a subtle white stroke, outline, or glow around dark logos and dark text-in-image so they stay visible when the background inverts. Prefer live HTML text over images of text, since text adapts to dark mode. Use the @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) media query to define dark-mode-specific styling in clients that support it, and use targeting hooks like [data-ogsc] for Outlook.com partial-invert support. Ensure high contrast ratios that meet WCAG standards in both modes. Test every email across the clients your audience uses before sending, because you cannot rely on one client's behavior to predict another's.

title: Reasons to Test Every Email Before You Send (Litmus)
text:
## Why pre-send testing matters

Every email client and device renders HTML email differently, and clients change constantly, so an email that looked fine yesterday can break today. Litmus research has found there can be a very large number of potential renderings for a single email across the combinations of clients, devices, and settings, and that the most popular email clients made a change on average every 1.2 days. Clients also drop support for HTML and CSS attributes without notice; for example Outlook.com dropped support for the margin property, and a Yahoo Mail update introduced a bug with the align attribute.

## What to check before sending

Rendering across the clients and devices your audience actually uses. Broken links: masked URLs are hard to verify by eye, so confirm each link goes to the right landing page with the correct UTM parameters. Images and alt text: because many subscribers have images blocked by default, every image needs descriptive alt text so the message survives without images. Preview pane elements: the from name, reply-to, subject line, and preview text, since subscribers spend only a few seconds deciding whether to open. Spelling and grammar, because there is no undo after sending. Dynamic and personalized content, including fallbacks for missing subscriber data. Plain-text version of multipart MIME messages. Dark mode rendering. Accessibility. Deliverability and spam checks.

## The ROI case

Litmus reports that email programs which test every email they send generate an average return on investment of 40 to 1, compared with an average of 34 to 1 for programs that never test. Testing turns email from a risky one-shot broadcast into a reliable channel.

title: Email List Segmentation (Mailchimp)
text:
## What segmentation is

Email segmentation is the process of dividing and separating email subscribers into groups or segments based on criteria like age, location, and behavior, so you can send each group content that matches what they actually care about, rather than blasting one message to everyone.

## Why it matters

Relevance and engagement: sending emails that match a group's interests leads to more opens and clicks. Deliverability: targeted content gets more opens and clicks, which tells mailbox providers (ISPs) your emails are wanted, improving sender reputation, and it reduces spam complaints and unsubscribes. ROI: better targeting drives higher conversion rates and higher revenue from the email channel.

## Common segmentation criteria

Demographics: age, gender, income, family status. Behavior: purchase history, website visits, cart abandonment, and product interest. Geography: country, region, city, and time zone (useful for send-time and localization). Email activity: open and click rates and overall engagement level, which lets you separate highly engaged subscribers from those who are going cold. Funnel or lifecycle stage: awareness, consideration, decision, and retention. For B2B, organization type such as company size and industry, and customer type such as B2B versus B2C.

## Putting it to work

Start with the data you already collect at signup and through engagement, build a few high-value segments (for example new subscribers, engaged buyers, and lapsing subscribers), and tailor content, offers, and cadence to each. Combine segmentation with automation so the right message reaches the right segment at the right moment in the customer journey.

title: Email Drip Campaigns: Examples and Best Practices (Mailchimp)
text:
## What a drip campaign is

A drip campaign is a marketing strategy that sends an automated sequence of emails when certain conditions are met. Messages are triggered by a specific action (such as signing up, downloading a resource, or attending a demo) or by inactivity, and they are scheduled in advance so subscribers are not overwhelmed all at once. Drip campaigns are also called lifecycle emails, automated email campaigns, or automated marketing.

## Common types

Welcome emails: sent to new subscribers or first-time customers to introduce the brand and set expectations. Onboarding sequences: educate new users and drive them to activation. Lead nurturing: guide prospects through the funnel with educational, trust-building content. Product recommendations: personalized suggestions based on browsing or purchase history. Abandoned cart: reminders, often with urgency or an incentive, for shoppers who did not complete checkout. Re-engagement or reactivation: win back subscribers who have gone quiet.

## How they work and best practices

Drip campaigns differ from a one-off newsletter because they target specific segments based on demographics, behaviors, and triggered actions. A common structure is roughly 4 to 10 emails spaced anywhere from 4 days to 2 weeks apart, depending on the goal. Benefits include moving contacts through the funnel to boost conversions, saving time through automation, increasing engagement with timely and relevant content, and re-engaging inactive contacts. Personalization matters: Mailchimp cites that 60% of online shoppers would not stay loyal to brands that send non-personalized content, so match the message to where the subscriber is in their journey.

title: A Winning Welcome Email Series (Mailchimp)
text:
## Why welcome emails matter

The welcome email is the first message a new subscriber receives, sent right after they sign up, when their interest and attention are highest. It sets the tone for the relationship, confirms the subscription, and is one of the highest-performing message types in email marketing.

## Performance statistics

Mailchimp reports that a welcome email series generates an average of 51% more revenue than a single welcome email. In one example, the retailer ban.do's welcome series achieved a combined average open rate of 38.6%, with the first email alone reaching a 51.7% open rate, far above typical promotional open rates.

## Structure and timing

Welcome emails typically send about one day after subscription, though the delay can be customized, and many brands send the first message immediately. A series lets you spread the job across several messages instead of cramming everything into one. Ban.do's three-email series is a useful model: an initial offer email (a 10% off coupon), a social media engagement email, and a re-engagement email that is sent only to subscribers who have not yet purchased.

## Best practices

Give each email in the series a single clear purpose, introducing the brand, building the relationship, then driving conversion. Personalize with the subscriber's name and reference the action they took. Keep the first impression email short: welcome them and point to the next step rather than overwhelming them. Segment different audiences into different series (for example wholesale versus retail). Condition later emails on behavior so you do not keep messaging people who have already converted.

title: Subject Line Testing and A/B Testing (Mailchimp)
text:
## Why subject lines matter

The subject line is the first thing recipients see and often determines whether they open or ignore the message, so it is one of the highest-leverage elements to optimize. Small improvements in subject lines compound into meaningful gains in open rate and downstream clicks and conversions.

## How A/B testing subject lines works

Create multiple versions of an email that are identical in every way except the subject line, then send each version to a randomized portion of your subscribed audience. Mailchimp automatically measures which subject line wins on open rate and sends that winner to the remainder of the list. The keys to a valid test are randomizing the groups to avoid bias and testing only one variable at a time, so you know exactly which change caused the difference. Multivariate testing (testing several elements at once) generally requires a larger list to reach statistically significant results.

## Sample size

Mailchimp requires a minimum of 10% of your list for the test portion, but recommends at least 5,000 subscribers per variation (about 10,000 total across two variations) for reliable results, because small samples produce noisy winners.

## What makes a good subject line

Keep it brief, ideally under about 50 characters so it is not truncated on mobile (60 characters or fewer is a common ceiling). Personalize with merge tags such as the recipient's name or location. Use no more than 1 emoji and use it to supplement, not replace, words. Questions and numbers can lift open rates. Convey the value proposition clearly and keep a consistent brand voice. Avoid spam trigger words such as free, win, and cash, which can hurt both open rates and deliverability.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Email Accessibility (Litmus)
text:
## Why email accessibility matters

Accessible email lets everyone, including people who use screen readers, have low vision, are colorblind, or have dyslexia, understand and act on your message. Litmus cites that roughly one in four US adults and one in six people globally have a disability, that vision impairments affect around 2.2 billion people worldwide, that color blindness affects about 8% of men, and that dyslexia affects around 15% of people. People with disabilities also control over 1 trillion dollars in annual disposable income, so accessibility expands reach and, through higher engagement, supports deliverability. WCAG guidelines also underpin legal requirements such as the ADA, the UK Equality Act, and the European Accessibility Act.

## Semantic structure

Use real semantic HTML: p tags for paragraphs and h1 through h6 for a logical heading hierarchy (h1 primary, h2 secondary, and so on) so screen reader users can scan by header. Add role="presentation" (and aria-hidden where appropriate) to layout tables so screen readers treat them as layout, not data.

## Images, text, and color

Provide descriptive alt text that conveys each image's purpose in context; use a null alt attribute (alt="") only for purely decorative images. Prefer live HTML text over images of text, since live text supports screen readers, scales with zoom, and adapts to dark mode. Meet WCAG AA color contrast, a minimum ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text, and check it with a tool such as WebAIM's Color Contrast Checker. Use a minimum font size around 14px on desktop and 16px on mobile, set line-height to about 1.5, avoid justified text, and use descriptive link text instead of generic "click here." Make tap targets large enough for touch, a minimum of about 44 by 44 pixels.
